## Variable Selection by VIF

```{r vif-r2-overfitted-model}
# an R-squared of 0.7347 for 36 predictors 
overfitted_model <- lm(burnout ~., data = raw_data)
summary(overfitted_model)$r.squared

variance_inflation_factors <- tibble(
  variables = character(36),
  values = numeric(36)
)

for (i in 1:36) {
  variance_inflation_factors$values[i] <- vif(overfitted_model)[[i]]
  variance_inflation_factors$variables[i] <- names(vif(overfitted_model))[[i]]
}

variance_inflation_factors <- variance_inflation_factors %>%
  mutate(VIF_range = ifelse(values > 4, "4-5", ifelse(values < 4 & values > 3, "3-4", ifelse(values < 3 & values > 2, "2-3", ifelse(values < 2 & values > 1, "1-2", "less than 1")))))

variance_inflation_factors %>%
  arrange(desc(values))

ggplot(variance_inflation_factors, aes(x = VIF_range, color = VIF_range)) + geom_bar() + scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(4,5,12,15)) + labs(title = str_wrap("Binned Variance Inflation Factors for predicting burnout with all variables in the 'raw data'", width = 45), x = "VIF range", legend = "VIF range")
```

```{r reduced-vif-model}
# fitting a model with the variance inflation factors restricted from 1-3
variance_inflation_factors_reduced <- variance_inflation_factors %>%
  filter(VIF_range %in% c("1-2", "2-3"))
raw_data_reduced <- raw_data %>% select(variance_inflation_factors_reduced$variables, burnout)

lm.reduced <- lm(burnout ~., data = raw_data_reduced)

summary(lm.reduced)$r.squared

# this model has 20 predictors, and the variables with the higher-end of
# the variance inflation factors have been removed

vif(lm.reduced)
```

```{r}
summary(lm.reduced)
```

## Variable Selection by Significance

If we take the predictors that are considered to be significant under the standard 0.05 threshold with the model that only contains the variables with variance inflation factors less than 3 from the original 36 predictor model, then we would fit a model on 'physical', 'meaning purpose', 'apathetic', and motivated'

```{r reduced-model}
# to be clear, this model takes the significant predictors (p>0.05) for the model
# of reduced variance inflation (cutting the 3+ threshold) from the 36 
# predictor model
lm.reduced.sig <- lm(burnout ~ physical + meaning_purpose + apathetic, data = raw_data_reduced)
summary(lm.reduced.sig)$r.squared
```

```{r}

# these variables are those that were listed to be 'statistically significant' from the model that they fit, where their p-values for the t-test for each variable
# was less than .05

fitted_variables <- raw_data %>% select(burnout,apathetic, self_compassion, compassion_fatigue, mental_wellbeing,depression,receptive,connectedness, worry, dissociation, perception)

# fitting a regression model from which the R^2 values were obtained

fitted.lm <- lm(burnout ~., data = fitted_variables)

summary(fitted.lm)$r.squared

sig_variables <- raw_data %>% select(burnout,apathetic, self_compassion, compassion_fatigue, mental_wellbeing,depression,receptive,connectedness)
```

Looking at the original paper

- The **burnout variable** is considered to be the response variable

- their first multiple linear regression model is fit using the variables that have p-values under 0.05 for t-tests regarding whether the value of the coefficient is non-zero or not

  - these people do not seem to be treating the 0.05 significance level like a 'night' and 'day' thing

- they use the variables *apathetic*, *self compassion*, *compassion fatigue*, *mental wellbeing*, *depression*, *receptive*, and *connectedness*

- the $R^2$ in their model is 0.70, and they say that 70% of the variation in burnout scores is explained by the regressors, but again, this does not tell us anything about the appropriateness of the model fit.

  - a good question to address is whether they are still overfitting their regression model after removing the non-significant predictors--worry, dissociation, and perception--

The predictor variables are:

- burnout
- apathetic
- compassion_fatigue
- mental_wellbeing
- depression
- receptive
- connectedness

Removed variables that are not considered to be 'statistically significant'

- this includes 'worry,' 'dissociation,', and 'perception'
- the authors of the article mentioned that the predictors explain about 70% of the variation in burnout (when including the 'non-statistically significant' predictors)

# Sam

## Analysis of Covariance

```{r ancova-eda}
# Package used according to the authors
library(jmv)

# Plot self compassion and compassion fatigue as variables of interest
sig_variables |>
  select(self_compassion, compassion_fatigue) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), 
               names_to = "Variable", 
               values_to = "Values") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = Values), binwidth = 2, color = "blue") +
  labs(
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free_y")
```

Neither of these histograms match the one reported in the paper (S1 Fig), but the compassion_fatigue plot comes much closer, suggesting the authors may have mixed up the names of the variables in their reporting. Unfortunately, since they use this plot to justify binning one variable over another, it's unclear if their code matches what they described or what they said they did. We replicate with both options

### Bin self_compassion (as reported)

Note, it is not clear from the paper why the variables that are included in the ANCOVA model are selected. I have based my selection here on the paper's reported results.

```{r}
# Bin self compassion and select reported variables
ancova_data <- raw_data |>
  select(worry, apathetic, self_compassion, curious,
         fear_of_harm_from_others, avoidance, compassion_fatigue,
         dissociation, perception, mental_wellbeing, depression,
         receptive, connectedness, burnout) |>
  mutate(
    self_compassion_binned = case_when(
      self_compassion <= -4 ~ "low",
      self_compassion >= 4 ~ "high",
      TRUE ~ "medium"
    ),
    self_compassion_binned = as.factor(self_compassion_binned)
  ) |>
  select(-c(self_compassion))

# Fit ANCOVA Model
ancova_model <- jmv::ancova(
  formula = burnout ~ .,
  data = ancova_data)

# Look at results
ancova_model$main
```

### Bin compassion_fatigue (based on dist. description)

```{r}
# Bin self compassion and select reported variables
ancova_data <- raw_data |>
  select(worry, apathetic, self_compassion, curious,
         fear_of_harm_from_others, avoidance, compassion_fatigue,
         dissociation, perception, mental_wellbeing, depression,
         receptive, connectedness, burnout) |>
  mutate(
    compassion_fatigue_binned = case_when(
      compassion_fatigue <= -4 ~ "low",
      compassion_fatigue >= 4 ~ "high",
      TRUE ~ "medium"
    ),
    compassion_fatigue_binned = as.factor(compassion_fatigue_binned)
  ) |>
  select(-c(compassion_fatigue))

# Fit ANCOVA Model
ancova_model <- jmv::ancova(
  formula = burnout ~ .,
  data = ancova_data)

# Look at results
ancova_model$main
```

## ANCOVA Conclusion

Findings could not be even remotely replicated. The paper indicates that "all the variables except worry and perception have a p-value below 0.05," but based on our model, only `worry`, `apathetic`, and `avoidance` are the significant variables. Also, when discussing ANCOVA, the paper indicates that only one dependent variable should be binned, but notably `depression`, `receptive`, and `connectedness` are all binary (and thus categorical) variables.

# Zack

## Repeated five-fold cross-validation

```{r first repeated-five-fold-cv}
set.seed(6950)

# Use the same response, predictors, and rows as Jack's 10-predictor model.
cv_data <- model.frame(fitted.lm)
cv_formula <- formula(fitted.lm)

fold_r2 <- matrix(
  NA_real_, nrow = 10, ncol = 5,
  dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("Fold_", 1:5))
)

for (r in 1:10) {
  fold_id <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(cv_data)))

  for (f in 1:5) {
    train <- cv_data[fold_id != f, , drop = FALSE]
    test  <- cv_data[fold_id == f, , drop = FALSE]

    fit <- lm(cv_formula, data = train)
    predicted <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
    fold_r2[r, f] <- cor(predicted, test$burnout)^2
  }
}

cv_results <- data.frame(
  Repetition = 1:10,
  fold_r2,
  Mean_R2 = rowMeans(fold_r2)
)

knitr::kable(cv_results, digits = 3)
```

Across the ten repetitions, the mean validation $R^2$ for the 10-predictor model was `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(cv_results$Mean_R2))`.

The five-fold cross-validation (CV) above uses Jack's fitted model created in accordance with the researcher's strategy of choosing regressors based on p-value. However, in the methodology section where the researchers discuss the use of 5-fold CV, they do not make it clear whether they are using such a model (with 10 regressors) or the model that they discuss right before in Table 2, which has 13 regressors ("curious", "fear-of-harm-from-others", and "avoidance" are included in this 13-regressor model). As such, I will also run another 5-fold CV on the model including those three additional regressors to see if I can get closer to the published result:

```{r table2-repeated-five-fold-cv}

# Add the three Table 2 predictors missing from the 10-predictor model
formula_13 <- update(
  formula(fitted.lm),
  . ~ . + curious + fear_of_harm_from_others + avoidance
)

table2_fit <- lm(formula_13, data = raw_data)
cv_data_13 <- model.frame(table2_fit)

# Confirm both models use the same diary entries in the same order.
stopifnot(identical(rownames(cv_data_13), rownames(model.frame(fitted.lm))))

# Use the same seed and fold assignment method as the 10-predictor chunk.
set.seed(6950)

fold_r2_13 <- matrix(
  NA_real_, nrow = 10, ncol = 5,
  dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("Fold_", 1:5))
)

for (r in 1:10) {
  fold_id <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(cv_data_13)))
  
  for (f in 1:5) {
    train <- cv_data_13[fold_id != f, , drop = FALSE]
    test  <- cv_data_13[fold_id == f, , drop = FALSE]
    
    fit <- lm(formula_13, data = train)
    predicted <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
    fold_r2_13[r, f] <- cor(predicted, test$burnout)^2
  }
}

cv_results_13 <- data.frame(
  Repetition = 1:10,
  fold_r2_13,
  Mean_R2 = rowMeans(fold_r2_13)
)

knitr::kable(cv_results_13, digits = 3,
             caption = "Five-fold validation results for the 13-predictor model")

cv_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Group model (10 predictors)", "Table 2 model (13 predictors)"),
  Mean_CV_R2 = c(mean(cv_results$Mean_R2), mean(cv_results_13$Mean_R2))
)

knitr::kable(cv_comparison, digits = 4,
             caption = "Mean validation R-squared across the same folds")
```

Using the same diary entries and folds, adding `curious`, `fear_of_harm_from_others`, and `avoidance` changed the mean validation $R^2$ from `r sprintf("%.4f", mean(cv_results$Mean_R2))` to `r sprintf("%.4f", mean(cv_results_13$Mean_R2))`. The published mean was 0.7103.

Using the same five folds in each of the ten repetitions for both models, we obtained a mean validation $R^2$ of `r sprintf("%.4f", mean(cv_results$Mean_R2))` for the 10-predictor model and `r sprintf("%.4f", mean(cv_results_13$Mean_R2))` for the 13-predictor model. Adding curiosity, fear of harm from others, and avoidance changed the mean score by `r sprintf("%+.4f", mean(cv_results_13$Mean_R2) - mean(cv_results$Mean_R2))` (13-predictor minus 10-predictor). Because both models predicted the same held-out diary entries, this difference reflects the change in predictors.

## 5-fold Cross-Validation Conclusion

Our closer reconstruction of Table 2, using all 13 named predictors and the spreadsheet as released, produced a mean validation score `r sprintf("%.4f", abs(mean(cv_results_13$Mean_R2) - 0.7103))` away from the published mean of 0.7103. In keeping with the above histograms and ANCOVA results, this shows that following the reported methods with the released data did not reproduce every published result. The paper reports the average score for each repetition, but the original fold assignments are unavailable, so we cannot determine how much of the remaining CV difference is due to the choice of folds.

## Correlation Matrix

```{r}
# creating the correlation matrix for the fitted model with the variables deemed
# significant under the 36-variable model

# this is the response variable: burnout
Y <- sig_variables$burnout
# here is the matrix for the predictors for the model, including the intercept
X.mat <- cbind(rep(1, nrow(sig_variables)), sig_variables$apathetic, sig_variables$self_compassion, sig_variables$compassion_fatigue, sig_variables$mental_wellbeing, sig_variables$depression, sig_variables$receptive, sig_variables$connectedness)

# here is the matrix for the estimates of the coefficients
beta.hat <- solve(t(X.mat) %*% X.mat) %*% t(X.mat) %*% Y; #beta.hat
# calculating degrees of freedom; rows-columns
df <- nrow(X.mat) - ncol(X.mat)
# calculating the residual sums of squares for the model
RSS <- t(Y-X.mat %*% beta.hat) %*% (Y-X.mat %*% beta.hat)
# calculating sigma.hat
sigma.hat <- as.numeric(sqrt(RSS/df))
# this is the covariance matrix
# recall that the variance for each of the predictors
# are on the diagonals
covariance_matrix <- sigma.hat^2*solve(t(X.mat) %*% X.mat); #covariance_matrix

# obtaining the standard errors for the beta hats

# here are the standard errors for the beta.hats
diagonal_matrix <- as.matrix(sqrt(diag(covariance_matrix)))

# specifying that n=8, the number of rows from the covariance matrix
n <- nrow(covariance_matrix)

diagonal_matrix

```

```{r}
# coding a correlation matrix

correlation_matrix <- matrix(NA, nrow = 8, ncol = 8)

# this is a for-loop to create a correlation

# this can be shortened if a function is written?

for (i in 1:8) {
  for (j in 1:8) {
    correlation_matrix[i,j] <- covariance_matrix[i,j] <- covariance_matrix[i,j]/sqrt(covariance_matrix[i,i]*covariance_matrix[j,j])
  }
}



# visual display for correlation; one using the 'correlation package'
# this first one is without the numeric variables

display.matrix <- cor_lower(correlation(sig_variables, redundant = TRUE))

if (require("ggplot2")) {
  ggplot(display.matrix, aes(x = Parameter2, y = Parameter1, fill = r)) +
    geom_tile() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)) + labs(title = "Correlation Matrix")
  
}

# this is done using the corrplot and the 'see' packages
cor_matrix <- cor(sig_variables)
corrplot(cor_matrix, method = 'number', type = 'lower',diag = FALSE, tl.cex = 0.8, number.cex = 0.8, cl.cex = 0.8, title = "Correlation Matrix for \"Significant\" predictors")
```
